title: Web Applications and Services
text:
Preface
This textbook is a self-study resource for the theoretical component of Web Applications and Services (ASW), Master’s in Electrical and Computer Engineering (MEEC), covering Web application architecture, best development practices, the HTTP protocol, HTML and CSS, server-side and client-side programming, database access, and REST Web Services, with Java EE as the case study.

title: Web Applications and Services
text:
Organisation
The textbook is organised into three thematic blocks:

Web Foundations — client-server architecture, HTML, CSS and the HTTP protocol
Classic Java EE — Servlets, the stateful model and session management
Web Services — security and filters, and REST Web Services, including consuming an API from JavaScript in the browser

The practical LABs (the same as ESIGELEC’s, with a JavaScript front-office added in LAB6) are described in Appendices D1 to D6, with the development environment setup in Appendix C.

title: 1  Web Application Architecture
text:
1.1 The Problem: Building a Web Application from Scratch
A Web application is not simply a program that runs on a single computer: it is a program that answers requests coming from multiple clients, simultaneously, over the network. Built from scratch, with no supporting platform, an application of this kind would have to solve, on its own, a set of problems common to any system of this sort:
Solving all of these problems again and again, application after application, would be a waste of effort. This is exactly why enterprise platforms exist, providing these services ready to use, and freeing developers to focus on the business logic of the application.

title: 1  Web Application Architecture
text:
1.2 Two Orientations: Presentation vs. Service
A Web application can follow two distinct orientations, depending on the kind of response it produces:

Presentation-oriented

Generates interactive Web pages (HTML, CSS and dynamic content) in response to each request. This is the traditional Web application model, meant to be consumed directly by a human user through a browser.

Service-oriented

Implements the endpoint of a Web service, typically returning structured data in JSON or XML format instead of HTML. This model is meant to be consumed by another program: a mobile application, a single-page application, or another service.


This distinction largely maps onto the split between front-end (the part of the application that interacts directly with whoever uses it) and back-end (the part that processes logic and data). A presentation-oriented application tends to blend these two responsibilities into a single server-side component; a service-oriented application separates them clearly, leaving the front-end entirely up to the client.

title: 1  Web Application Architecture
text:
1.3 The MVC Pattern
Organising all of an application’s code as a single undifferentiated block quickly becomes unmanageable: the code that processes the request, the code that accesses data, and the code that generates the response end up tangled together, hard to test or change independently. The Model-View-Controller (MVC) pattern solves this by splitting the application into three distinct responsibilities:

Model

Represents the application’s data and business logic, independently of how it is presented. In a Web application, the Model is typically responsible for accessing the database and returning already-validated information.

View

Responsible for presenting the data to whoever requests it, without containing business logic. In a presentation-oriented application, the View generates HTML; in a service-oriented application, there is, in fact, no server-side View at all: the response is just structured data (JSON), and it is the client that decides how to present it.

Controller

Receives the request, decides which operation to perform on the Model, and chooses the View (or response format) to return. The Controller is what bridges the incoming HTTP request and the application’s logic.


This separation of responsibilities is one of the most recurring design principles throughout this subject. It shows up in its classic form when a server-side component acts as Controller and delegates presentation to another, which acts as View; and it shows up in a far less obvious form when the View stops existing on the server side and is instead rebuilt in the browser, from JSON data.

title: 1  Web Application Architecture
section: 1.4 Three Pieces: Frontend, Middleware and Backend
text:
1.4 Three Pieces: Frontend, Middleware and Backend
Both the presentation/service distinction and the MVC pattern describe the same central idea, seen from different angles: a Web application is not a single block, but a set of pieces with distinct roles, communicating with one another. Throughout this course, those pieces always reduce to the same three:

Frontend

The part of the application that runs on the client side (typically a browser), responsible for presenting information and collecting input from whoever uses it. It largely corresponds to the View in MVC.

Middleware

The protocol that connects the Frontend to the Backend, carrying requests and responses between the two. In this course, that protocol is always HTTP.

Backend

The part of the application that runs on the server side, responsible for business logic and data access. It largely corresponds to the Model and the Controller in MVC.


This three-way division is the map for the rest of this book: first the Frontend is built (Chapter 2, in HTML/CSS/Bootstrap), then the Middleware that connects it to the server is studied in detail (Chapter 3, networking and the HTTP protocol), and only then is the Backend built that actually answers those requests (from Chapter 4 onward, with Servlets and, later, REST APIs).

title: 1  Web Application Architecture
text:
1.5 The Client-Server Model
The Middleware connecting the Frontend to the Backend rests on the client-server model: the Frontend (typically a browser) sends a request over the network, and the Backend processes that request and returns a response.






Figure 1.1: The client (for example, a browser) sends an HTTP request; the server processes it and returns a response. The exchange repeats at every interaction, without the server, by itself, retaining memory of the previous one.



This exchange takes place through the HTTP protocol (HyperText Transfer Protocol), which has two fundamental characteristics:

It is transaction-oriented: each interaction consists of a request followed by a response
It is stateless: the server does not, by itself, retain any memory of a client’s previous requests

The absence of state at the protocol level does not prevent an application from needing to retain information across requests (for instance, to know that a user is authenticated). That need is addressed at the application level, not the protocol level, through mechanisms such as sessions and cookies (see Chapter 5).
The details of this protocol, the Middleware connecting these two pieces, are the subject of Chapter 3.

title: 3  From the Network to HTTP
text:
3.1 The Middleware Connecting Frontend and Backend
Chapter 1 identified three components in any Web application: Frontend, Middleware and Backend. Chapter 2 was devoted to the first of these, a set of HTML pages with forms, including the capital-lookup form (capital.html) and the authentication form (login.html). On their own, these forms do nothing: they need a protocol to carry the data the user fills in to a server, and to bring a response back. That protocol, the Middleware used in Web applications, is HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol).
HTTP, however, does not work alone. For a request to leave the browser and reach a server, possibly on the other side of the world, HTTP relies on two other protocols: TCP, which delivers the data to the right application, and IP, which gets it to the right machine. This chapter follows that path in order: it starts from the client-server model, goes down to the transport and network layers to show where ports and IP addresses come in, and only then details how HTTP works.

title: 3  From the Network to HTTP
text:
3.2 The Client-Server Model
All communication on the Web rests on the client-server model. In this model there are two clearly distinct roles:

Server

A program that is permanently listening, waiting for requests. It never takes the initiative to contact anyone: it simply responds to whoever contacts it. A single server handles requests from many different clients at the same time. In this course, the server is Apache Tomcat.

Client

A program that takes the initiative: it sends a request to the server and waits for the response. On the Web, the client is typically a browser (Chrome, Firefox, Safari), but it can be any program capable of sending requests, such as curl on the command line or a mobile app.








Figure 3.1: The client (for example, a browser) sends an HTTP request; the server processes it and returns a response. The exchange repeats with every interaction, without the server, on its own, keeping any memory of the previous one.



The interaction is always the same: the client sends a request, the server processes it and returns a response. This request-response pair is the basic unit of all communication on the Web: loading a page, submitting a form or fetching an image are each one or more of these exchanges.
For this exchange to happen, the client needs to answer two questions before sending anything:

On which machine is the server? The answer is an IP address, handled by the Internet layer.
Which program, inside that machine, should receive the request? A single machine may have several servers running at the same time (a Web server, a database server, a mail server). The answer is a port number, handled by the Transport layer.

Only once these two questions are settled does HTTP come in, defining what is said: the format of the request and of the response. The following sections explain how these three pieces fit together.

title: 3  From the Network to HTTP
text:
3.3 The TCP/IP Model
Network communications are organised in layers. Each layer provides a service to the layer immediately above and uses the services of the layer immediately below, without needing to know how those other layers work internally. The TCP/IP model, used on the Internet, organises the communications stack into four layers:









Layer
Responsibility
Addressing
Example protocols




Application
The format of the data exchanged between applications
URL
HTTP, FTP, SMTP, DNS


Transport
Delivery of data to the right process, reliably (TCP) or not (UDP)
Port
TCP, UDP


Internet
Routing of data between networks, to the right machine
IP address
IP


Network Access
Physical transmission of data over the local medium
MAC address
Ethernet, Wi-Fi









Figure 3.2: The four-layer TCP/IP model. HTTP lives at the Application layer, and rests on TCP (Transport layer) to guarantee that data arrives reliably and in the correct order.




3.3.1 Encapsulation
When the browser sends a request, the data travels down the stack, from the Application layer to the Network Access layer. At each layer a header of its own is added, with the information that layer needs. This process is called encapsulation (Figure 3.3):

Application: the browser builds the HTTP message (for example, GET /capital?countrycode=PT). From the point of view of the lower layers, this data is just the payload.
Transport: TCP adds a header whose most important information is the source and destination ports. The result is called a TCP segment.
Internet: IP adds a header whose most important information is the source and destination IP addresses. The result is called an IP packet.
Network Access: the network card adds a header with the physical (MAC) addresses and, at the end, a check code (FCS, Frame Check Sequence) that lets the receiver detect whether the frame was corrupted along the way. The result is called a frame, which is then converted into electrical, optical or radio signals.







Figure 3.3: Encapsulation of an HTTP request. Each layer receives from the layer above a unit of data that it treats as payload, without reading it (light blue), and adds its own header to it (orange): the ports in the TCP segment, the IP addresses in the IP packet and the MAC addresses in the Ethernet frame. The dashed red line marks the socket (IP address + port), the boundary where the application hands the data over to TCP (see Section 3.4).



On reception, the process is reversed: each layer checks the header that concerns it, strips it off and passes the rest to the layer above. The Internet layer confirms that the destination IP address is the machine’s own; the Transport layer checks whether any application is registered on the destination port and, if so, hands it the data; finally, the Application layer receives the HTTP message exactly as the browser wrote it.
HTTP is therefore an Application-layer protocol: it is not concerned with how the data reaches its destination, it only defines the format of the request and of the response. That delivery is the job of the lower layers, the two most relevant of which for Web development are described next.

section: 3.4 The Transport Layer: TCP and Ports
text:
3.4 The Transport Layer: TCP and Ports

3.4.1 Ports
An IP address identifies a machine, but many programs run on a machine at the same time. The port is the number that identifies, within a machine, the program the data is meant for. When a server starts, it registers on a port and starts listening: every TCP segment arriving with that destination port is delivered to it.
Ports are integers between 0 and 65535, divided into three ranges:








Range
Name
Use




0 to 1023
Well-known ports
Reserved for standard services


1024 to 49151
Registered ports
Assigned to specific applications


49152 to 65535
Dynamic (ephemeral) ports
Temporarily assigned to clients



Some ports come up particularly often:



Port
Service




21
FTP (file transfer)


22
SSH (secure remote access)


25
SMTP (sending email)


53
DNS (name resolution)


80
HTTP


443
HTTPS (encrypted HTTP)


3306
MySQL / MariaDB


8080
Alternative HTTP (Apache Tomcat’s default port)



When the destination port is the protocol’s well-known port, there is no need to write it in the URL: http://www.utad.pt and http://www.utad.pt:80 are exactly the same address, because the browser assumes port 80 for http and port 443 for https. Tomcat, on the other hand, listens on port 8080 by default, so the port must be given explicitly, which is why every address used in this course has the form http://localhost:8080/....
The client also uses a port: the source port. It is not chosen by the user; it is assigned automatically by the operating system, from the dynamic range, when the connection is opened. It is to this port that the server sends its response. This is why a browser with several tabs open on the same site can receive the responses for each of them without mixing them up: each connection has its own source port.
The pair formed by an IP address and a port is called a socket. A TCP connection is fully identified by two sockets: the client’s (for example, 192.168.1.20:51734) and the server’s (for example, 203.0.113.10:80).


3.4.2 TCP
TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) is the transport protocol used by HTTP. Its job is to guarantee that data reaches its destination complete, error-free and in the order in which it was sent, even though the network underneath (IP) offers none of these guarantees. To do so, TCP:

Establishes a connection before sending data: client and server exchange three synchronisation messages (the so-called three-way handshake) and only then does the transfer begin. This is why TCP is said to be connection-oriented.
Numbers the segments: when the data is large, TCP splits it into several segments and gives each one a sequence number. The receiver uses these numbers to put them back in order and to detect whether any is missing.
Acknowledges receipt: the receiver replies to the sender with an acknowledgement of the segments received. If a segment is not acknowledged within a certain time, the sender sends it again.
Controls the flow: the sender adjusts how much data it sends at once to the receiver’s capacity and to the state of the network, so as not to overload them.

For Web developers, the practical consequence is simple: when the server reads an HTTP request, it can rely on that request being complete and in the right order. All the complexity of dealing with losses and retransmissions is hidden inside TCP.
The alternative to TCP at the Transport layer is UDP (User Datagram Protocol), which also uses ports but does without the connection, the numbering and the acknowledgements. It is faster but does not guarantee delivery, and is used where losing the occasional packet is preferable to waiting for it to be retransmitted, such as voice calls, live video or DNS queries.

title: 3  From the Network to HTTP
section: 3.5 The Internet Layer: IP and Addresses
text:
3.5 The Internet Layer: IP and Addresses

3.5.1 IP Addresses
IP (Internet Protocol) is responsible for getting each packet to the destination machine, identified by its IP address. In version 4 of the protocol (IPv4), still the most common, an IP address is made up of four numbers between 0 and 255, separated by dots, such as 203.0.113.10 or 192.168.1.20. Each of these numbers takes up 8 bits, which makes an IPv4 address a 32-bit number, with about 4.3 billion possible combinations. That number proved insufficient for the growth of the Internet, and gave rise to IPv6, with 128-bit addresses written in hexadecimal (for example, 2001:db8::10), which today coexists with IPv4.






Addresses used in the examples



The public addresses that appear in this chapter (203.0.113.10, 2001:db8::10) and the name www.example.com do not belong to any real machine: they are part of blocks reserved by the Internet standards exclusively for documentation and examples (RFC 5737 and RFC 3849 for the addresses, RFC 2606 for the names). The addresses 192.168.1.20 and 127.0.0.1, by contrast, are real addresses, for private and loopback use respectively, and are explained below.


As with ports, some addresses are reserved for specific purposes:







Address or range
Use




127.0.0.1
Loopback: the machine itself (name localhost)


10.0.0.0 to 10.255.255.255
Private addresses (internal networks)


172.16.0.0 to 172.31.255.255
Private addresses (internal networks)


192.168.0.0 to 192.168.255.255
Private addresses (home and office networks)



The address 127.0.0.1 deserves special mention in this course. A request sent to localhost never leaves the machine: it goes down the communications stack and back up again on the same computer, where Tomcat receives it. This is what makes it possible to develop and test a complete Web application, client and server, on a single laptop and without an Internet connection.
Private addresses, in turn, are only valid within a local network. This is why a student’s laptop can have the address 192.168.1.20 at home and a different address on the university network. To communicate with the outside world, the local network’s router translates this private address into a public one, in a process called NAT (Network Address Translation).


3.5.2 Routing
Client and server are rarely on the same network. An IP packet sent from a student’s home to the UTAD server crosses several intermediate networks. In each of them, a device called a router reads the destination IP address, looks up its routing table and decides to which neighbouring network the packet should be forwarded. The packet thus moves forward, hop by hop, until it reaches the network where the server is.
This routing is done packet by packet, and IP gives no guarantee of delivery: a packet may be lost, arrive duplicated or arrive out of order relative to those sent before it. It is precisely to make up for these failures that TCP exists in the layer above.


3.5.3 DNS: From Names to Addresses
IP addresses are convenient for machines but hard for people to remember. This is why one types www.example.com in the browser and not 203.0.113.10. The network, however, only knows IP addresses: before it can send anything, the browser has to convert the name into the corresponding address.
This conversion is done by DNS (Domain Name System), a hierarchical system of servers distributed across the Internet. The browser asks DNS which IP address is associated with a name, and DNS replies with the address that the browser will then place in the IP header of the packets. The name localhost is a special case: it is resolved by the machine itself, directly to 127.0.0.1, without consulting any DNS server.






Asking DNS directly



The nslookup command, available on Windows, macOS and Linux, asks DNS the same question the browser does and shows the answer. In a terminal:
nslookup www.utad.pt
The answer shows the DNS server that was queried and, on the Address line, the IP address (or addresses, IPv4 and IPv6) associated with the name. Repeating the command with other names (for example, www.google.com) shows that a single name can be associated with several addresses. Note that nslookup always queries a DNS server, unlike the browser, which resolves localhost locally; the result of nslookup localhost therefore varies from system to system and is not a good example.

title: 3  From the Network to HTTP
text:
3.6 From URL to Connection
With the three layers in place, it is possible to follow everything that happens when the user submits the capital-lookup form and the browser has to access the address:
http://localhost:8080/capital?countrycode=PT
The URL itself contains the information each layer needs:








Part of the URL
Value
Layer that uses it




Protocol
http
Application: defines the protocol and the default port (80)


Host
localhost
Internet: converted into the IP address 127.0.0.1 (normally by DNS; for localhost, by the machine itself)


Port
8080
Transport: identifies Tomcat within the machine


Path and parameters
/capital?countrycode=PT
Application: identifies the resource requested from the server



From here on, the sequence is always the same:

The browser extracts the host name from the URL and obtains its IP address (through DNS or, for localhost, directly).
The browser opens a TCP connection to the server’s socket, 127.0.0.1:8080. The operating system assigns the client a source port from the dynamic range.
The browser writes the HTTP request message and hands it to TCP, which splits it into segments, adds the ports and passes it to IP, which adds the addresses.
On the server side, the packets go up the stack: IP recognises its own address, TCP reassembles the message and hands it to the program registered on port 8080, Tomcat.
Tomcat processes the request and writes the HTTP response, which travels the reverse path to the browser’s source port.
The browser reads the response and displays it to the user.

Steps 1, 2 and 4 are handled entirely by the operating system and the network; steps 3, 5 and 6, as far as the content of the message is concerned, are defined by HTTP. It is this content, what the client asks for and what the server replies, that the rest of this chapter details.

title: 3  From the Network to HTTP
text:
3.7 HTTP
HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is a text-based protocol, based on the request-response model: the client sends a request, the server returns a response, and the connection between the two retains no memory of previous requests. Each request is handled independently, that is, HTTP has no state (it is stateless). This section details the three aspects that define a request and a response: methods, the general message format, and status codes.

3.7.1 Methods
Every request from the client to the server is made in HTTP format and indicates, through a method, the operation intended for a given resource. The “resource” in the context of Web applications can be an html page, an image, a PDF, or any other item capable of being manipulated digitally:



Method
Typical semantics




GET
Retrieve a resource


POST
Create a resource


PUT
Update or replace a resource


DELETE
Remove a resource


HEAD
Retrieve headers only, no body



These five methods cover the vast majority of operations performed by a Web application; the first two (GET and POST) are by far the most common in Web pages, while PUT and DELETE become more important mainly in Web services.


3.7.2 Message Format
When the application on the client’s computer wants to communicate with the server, it activates the Application layer of the communications protocol stack, which formats the request according to the HTTP protocol. Both a request and the response that follows it share a similar general message structure:

A first line, differing between a request (method, URL and HTTP version) and a response (HTTP version, status code and reason)
A set of headers, carrying metadata about the message (for instance, the destination host, the content type, or its length)
An optional body, holding the actual data

A GET request typically has no body: all the data it carries goes in the URL itself, as parameters. A POST request carries its data in the message body, outside the URL.






Figure 3.4: The general format of an HTTP message: the first line (different for a request and a response), followed by the various groups of headers, and finally the body.




Example: From the Capital-Lookup Form to an HTTP Request
Recall the capital-lookup form built in Chapter 2 (capital.html):
<form method="GET" action="/capital">
  <label for="countrycode">Código do país</label>
  <input type="text" id="countrycode" name="countrycode">
  <button type="submit">Consultar</button>
</form>
This HTML code is displayed in the browser as shown in Figure 3.5:






Figure 3.5: The capital-lookup form (capital.html), as displayed in the browser.



When submitted (by clicking the Consultar button) with the value PT in the input, the browser generates the following GET HTTP request:

GET /capital?countrycode=PT HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:8080

Note that, because this is a GET method, the countrycode parameter is sent as part of the URL (after the ?), and there is no body in the message. If the same form used method="POST", the parameter would instead travel in the request body, and the URL would stay clean (/capital).
The server, upon processing this request, returns an HTTP response such as the following:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
{"country": "Portugal", "capital": "Lisboa", "ccode": "PT"}



Example: From the Authentication Form to a POST Request with a Body
Now recall the authentication form, also from Chapter 2 (login.html), with the fields user and pass:
<form method="POST" action="/login">
  <label for="user">Utilizador</label>
  <input type="text" id="user" name="user">
  <label for="pass">Palavra-passe</label>
  <input type="password" id="pass" name="pass">
  <button type="submit">Entrar</button>
</form>
This HTML code is displayed in the browser as shown in Figure 3.6:






Figure 3.6: The authentication form (login.html) in the browser, filled in with the user javaee and the password asw2026, which appears masked because the field is of type password.



When Entrar is clicked, the form filled in this way generates the following HTTP request, in which each field gives rise to a parameter named after its name attribute (user and pass):

POST /login HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:8080
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Content-Length: 21
user=javaee&pass=asw2026

Unlike the previous example, the parameters no longer go in the URL: they follow in the request body, after a blank line separating the headers from the body. This is why credentials and other sensitive data are typically sent via POST, never GET: a request body is not recorded in browser history or in the server’s log files, unlike URL parameters.
Upon successfully validating the credentials, the server returns an HTTP response. In this case it is a presentation-oriented application (see Chapter 1), so the response body carries HTML code for the browser to display; in a service-oriented application, it would carry JSON. The response looks like this:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html
<h1>Bem-vindo, javaee</h1>
<p>Sessão iniciada com sucesso.</p>




3.7.3 Status Codes
Every HTTP response includes a numeric status code, briefly indicating the outcome of the request. Codes are grouped into five categories, based on the leading digit:



Range
Category




1xx
Informational


2xx
Success


3xx
Redirection


4xx
Client error


5xx
Server error



Within these categories, a handful of codes come up particularly often when developing Web services:







Code
Meaning




200 OK
The request was processed successfully


201 Created
A new resource was successfully created


400 Bad Request
The request is malformed, or a required parameter is missing


401 Unauthorized
The request is not authenticated: the server does not know who the client is


403 Forbidden
The client is authenticated but lacks permission to access the resource


404 Not Found
The requested resource does not exist


500 Internal Server Error
An unhandled error occurred on the server side



Choosing the right status code for each situation is an essential part of designing a Web service: the code, by itself, conveys information the client can use to decide how to react, without needing to parse the response body.

title: 4  Java EE and Servlet Fundamentals
text:
4.1 The Jakarta EE Platform
With the Frontend built (Chapter 2) and the Middleware detailed (Chapter 3), the third piece identified in Chapter 1 is still missing: the Backend, which actually receives HTTP requests and answers them. It is the subject of this chapter and of the ones that follow.
Jakarta EE (formerly known as Java EE, until it was renamed in 2019; the current version is Jakarta EE 11, from June 2025) is a platform that provides a set of ready-to-use services and APIs to deal with the problems common to any Web application (see Chapter 1), freeing developers to concentrate on the application’s business logic.
The platform is based on the Java language and on the Java Virtual Machine (JVM), which means that any component written for Jakarta EE benefits from the portability and automatic memory management already known from the language.
crumbs: 4  Java EE and Servlet Fundamentals

title: 4  Java EE and Servlet Fundamentals
text:
4.2 Layered Architecture
The Jakarta EE platform organises an application according to a distributed model in several layers (tiers), each with a well-defined role and typically installed on different machines:








Layer
Where it lives
Typical components




Client Tier
Client machine
Web pages (browser), client applications


Web Tier
Jakarta EE server
Servlets, JavaServer Pages, Web Services


Business Tier
Jakarta EE server
Enterprise Beans (business logic)


EIS Tier (Enterprise Information System)
Database server
Databases, enterprise information systems



This separation into layers allows each component to evolve relatively independently of the others: changing the database does not require rewriting the business logic, and changing the client interface does not require changing the server.






Figure 4.1: The layered architecture of Jakarta EE: the client communicates only with the Web layer, which relies on the business layer and, through it, on the data. Tomcat, used in this course, covers only the Web layer; the business logic is implemented in ordinary Java classes (for example, the DAO), not in Enterprise Beans.









Tomcat is not a full Jakarta EE server



Apache Tomcat, used throughout this course, is a Servlet Container: it implements only the Web Tier (Servlets, JSP). It does not support Enterprise Beans or the Business Tier as such, unlike a full Jakarta EE application server (for example, WildFly, WebSphere or GlassFish). In practice, this means that the business logic which, in the formal architecture, would belong to the Business Tier is implemented here directly in ordinary Java classes, not in Enterprise Beans.

title: 4  Java EE and Servlet Fundamentals
text:
4.3 Why Servlets?
Implementing, from scratch, a Java program able to answer HTTP requests would mean solving, alone, a set of problems common to any Web server: interpreting the HTTP message received, managing several connections at the same time (each in its own thread), controlling the life cycle of the instances in memory, and packaging all of this in a format that an application server knows how to install and start.
A Servlet is a Java class that runs inside a Servlet Container (for example, Apache Tomcat) and automatically receives all this work already done:

Interpretation (parsing) of the HTTP request
Management of threads, one per request
Management of the Servlet’s own life cycle
Its own deployment model, packaged in a .war file (Web Application Archive)

In the layered architecture presented above, the Servlet Container corresponds to the Web Tier: that is where Servlets live, between the client and the business layer.






Figure 4.2: From the client’s point of view, a Servlet is just another destination for HTTP requests: a Java class, running on the server, that receives a request and returns a response.
crumbs: 4  Java EE and Servlet Fundamentals

title: 4  Java EE and Servlet Fundamentals
section: 4.4 The Life Cycle of a Servlet
text:
4.4 The Life Cycle of a Servlet
When a request is routed to a Servlet, the container always follows the same sequence (Figure 4.3):

If there is no instance of that Servlet in memory yet, the container loads the class, creates an instance and calls the init() method
For each request received, the container invokes the service() method, which dispatches to doGet(), doPost() or another method depending on the HTTP verb used, passing it the request and response objects
If the container needs to remove the Servlet (for example, when the server shuts down), it invokes the destroy() method







Figure 4.3: The life cycle of a Servlet: the container loads the class and creates the instance on the first request (or when the server starts), calls init() once, service() once per HTTP request, in its own thread, dispatching to doGet(), doPost(), etc. depending on the verb, and destroy() once, when the server shuts down or the application is removed.

text:
4.9 Servlets and the MVC Pattern: the View Is Missing
This course focuses mostly on web service applications, so the Servlets presented always return JSON: being service-oriented, they have, in fact, no View (see Chapter 1). This does not mean that the application cannot feed a graphical view; in that case the MVC model is used with the Servlet acting as Controller and feeding a web page indirectly through JSON. That web page is naturally built in HTML, but it needs script logic that extracts the necessary data from the JSON and places it in the right spots of the HTML page (see Chapter 8).
If the application is, from the start, presentation-oriented, however, the same Servlet acting as Controller can generate the HTML of the page (the View) directly, or it can delegate that responsibility to a dedicated page, using a technology known as JSP (JavaServer Pages), keeping MVC’s separation of responsibilities, as shown in Figure 4.6.






Figure 4.6: The MVC pattern with Servlets: the Servlet is the Controller and uses the Model (the DAO), which accesses the data. The View can be in two places: in a client (an HTML page with JavaScript, a mobile app), which receives data in JSON directly from the Servlet; or in the browser, which receives an HTML page generated on the server by a JSP, to which the Servlet forwards the request together with the data.



That dedicated page, the JavaServer Page (JSP), is covered in detail in Chapter 5.

title: 5  The Stateful Model: Sessions and JSP
text:
5.1 HTTP Is Stateless: the Problem
The HTTP protocol is stateless (see Chapter 3): each request is independent, and the server does not, by itself, keep any memory of previous requests. At protocol level, there is no notion of a “logged-in user”.
This raises an immediate practical problem: if a user authenticates in one request, how does a following request, minutes later, know that this user is still authenticated? The answer involves two complementary mechanisms:
crumbs: 5  The Stateful Model: Sessions and JSP

title: 5  The Stateful Model: Sessions and JSP
text:
Cookies: a small piece of information stored on the client side, automatically sent back by the browser with each following request
HttpSession: an object stored on the server side, associated with an identifier that the client sends back with each request
crumbs: 5  The Stateful Model: Sessions and JSP

title: 5  The Stateful Model: Sessions and JSP
crumbs: 5  The Stateful Model: Sessions and JSP

title: 5  The Stateful Model: Sessions and JSP
text:
5.3 Sessions (HttpSession)
Keeping state on the server side requires an object of its own: the HttpSession. The essential difference from a cookie lies in where the data is kept (Figure 5.1): the browser keeps only an identifier, and it is the server that keeps, associated with that identifier, all the session data. The data never leaves the server, and the client can neither read nor change it.






Figure 5.1: A cookie keeps the data on the client; a session keeps it on the server. In the case of the session, the browser only keeps the identifier (JSESSIONID), which works as the key to find the right session on the server.



A session is obtained, or created, from the request:
HttpSession session = request.getSession();          // creates one if it does not exist
HttpSession session = request.getSession(true);      // equivalent, explicit
HttpSession session = request.getSession(false);     // NEVER creates; returns null if there is none
Once obtained, the session stores and returns information through attributes, and can be ended explicitly:
session.setAttribute("email", "foo@fool.com");
String email = (String) session.getAttribute("email");
session.invalidate();                    // ends the session
session.setMaxInactiveInterval(1800);     // inactivity time, in seconds
session.getId();                          // session identifier (the JSESSIONID)
session.getAttributeNames();              // names of all the stored attributes
One piece is missing: if HTTP has no memory of previous requests, how does the server know that two successive requests belong to the same session? The answer is, again, cookies: by convention, the session identifier travels in a cookie called JSESSIONID, created automatically by the Servlet Container on the first call to getSession().

JSESSIONID=22562577CE80EF3B1DAAA0E48F2B6392

Figure 5.2 shows the complete mechanism, step by step:

The browser sends the credentials (POST /login). It does not yet have any cookie from this server.
The Servlet calls getSession(), the container creates a new session with a unique identifier, and the response carries the header Set-Cookie: JSESSIONID=....
In a following request (GET /perfil), the browser automatically sends the cookie back in the Cookie header. The container uses the identifier to find the right session among all those it keeps.
The Servlet reads the attributes of that session and answers with that user’s data.







Figure 5.2: The JSESSIONID cookie links successive requests to the same session. The identifier (here shortened to A3F9) is created by the server on the first request, sent to the browser with Set-Cookie and sent back by it, with Cookie, in all the following requests.



When the client does not accept cookies, there is an alternative: encoding the session identifier directly in the URL.

http://localhost:8080/loja/perfil;jsessionid=829F8836C240B51DD2F074259F242833

It is good practice to always call response.encodeURL(url) when building a destination URL: if cookies are enabled, the method returns the URL unchanged; if they are not, it automatically adds the jsessionid.

title: 5  The Stateful Model: Sessions and JSP
section: 5.5 The MVC Pattern with Servlet and JSP
text:
5.5 The MVC Pattern with Servlet and JSP
Chapter 1 presented the MVC pattern at a conceptual level, and Chapter 4 showed how a Servlet works as a Controller. The pages built in Chapter 2 already play the role of View, but they are static: their content does not change with the request. This section shows an alternative way of building the View, this time generated dynamically on the server side, from the data the Controller hands it.






Figure 5.3: The general MVC model, applicable to any interface (not only Web): the Controller updates the Model and the presentation; the View reads the Model to present itself.



In a presentation-oriented application, the Servlet receives the request and decides what to show, but delegates the actual generation of the HTML to a JavaServer Page (JSP). The Model, in turn, is an ordinary Java class (for example, a DAO), independent of both.
The Servlet is linked to the JSP through a RequestDispatcher: it places the data to show in a request attribute, and forwards the request itself to the page:
request.setAttribute("utilizador", utilizador);
request.getRequestDispatcher("/perfil.jsp").forward(request, response);
A forward is an internal hand-over: the Servlet passes the request to another component of the same server, without sending it back to the browser. The complete path of a request is shown in Figure 5.4:

The browser requests GET /perfil and the request reaches the Servlet.
The Servlet obtains the data (through the DAO) and stores it in the request, with request.setAttribute(...).
The Servlet hands perfil.jsp the same request object and the same response object it received.
The JSP reads the data from the request and writes the HTML into the response.
The browser receives a single response, and the address bar still shows /perfil.

Everything happens inside the server: there is a single HTTP request, and the browser never knows the JSP existed. That is why the attributes placed in the request by the Servlet are still available in the JSP: both components work on the same request object.






Figure 5.4: MVC with Servlet and JSP: (1) the request reaches the Servlet, the Controller; (2) the Servlet obtains the data from the Model (the DAO); (3) it places it in a request attribute and forwards the request to the JSP, the View; (4) the JSP generates the HTML that is returned to the browser.



A JSP is a text document that mixes two kinds of content: static HTML and dynamic script elements. The first time it is requested, the Servlet Container automatically converts it into a Servlet class, which from then on behaves exactly like any other Servlet, in the role of Controller.

The life cycle of a JSP follows the same model as the Servlet it is converted into (see Chapter 4), with two details of its own:

The container automatically recompiles the JSP whenever the .jsp file is changed
Instead of init() and destroy(), the JSP offers the jspInit() and jspDestroy() methods

Another practical difference: inside a JSP, a set of objects is automatically available, without any prior declaration; they are called implicit objects:

title: 6  Security and Filters
text:
6.1 The Problem: Security Repeated in Every Servlet
With what has been presented so far (see Chapter 5), authentication is solved: the LoginServlet validates the credentials and stores the user in the session, and each protected endpoint checks that session at the start of its doGet() or doPost(). This works, but it has a hidden cost: the authentication logic lives, duplicated, inside each protected Servlet.
This duplication brings several problems:
In other words, this duplication violates the DRY principle (Don’t Repeat Yourself): a responsibility should live in a single place, and repeated logic increases the maintenance cost whenever that logic needs to change. More precisely, this design violates the Single Responsibility Principle: each Servlet ends up with two distinct responsibilities, its own business logic and the security logic imposed on it. This makes security policies hard to evolve, and the design poorly scalable, both in number of endpoints and in the complexity of the access rules.

title: 6  Security and Filters
text:
The same session check is repeated in every protected endpoint
There is a real risk of inconsistency between those copies
It is easy to forget the protection when creating a new endpoint

title: 6  Security and Filters
6  Security and Filters
text:
6.3 What Is a Filter
The question still to answer is where the security logic should live: inside each Servlet? Duplicated across all endpoints? Or centralised in a single component? Security is, by nature, a cross-cutting concern: it runs through the whole application, instead of belonging to a single module. This is exactly what the Filter exists for.
A Filter is a server-side component that intercepts HTTP requests:

It runs before the target Servlet
It can also run after the Servlet (on the response)
It can block, redirect or modify the request or the response

Besides authentication and authorisation, Filters are the natural mechanism for other cross-cutting concerns: activity logging, CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing), or input validation. A Filter separates these concerns from the business logic, which stays exclusively in the Servlet.

title: 6  Security and Filters
section: 6.4 Where a Filter Sits in the Request
text:
6.4 Where a Filter Sits in the Request
One or more Filters can be chained between the client and the Servlet that actually handles the request. The request goes through the Filters in the order of the chain and only then reaches the Servlet, where the business logic lives; the response follows the reverse path, back to the client.






Figure 6.1: A request goes through the chain of Filters before reaching the Servlet; each Filter can block the request (red), modify it (yellow) or let it proceed (green, by calling chain.doFilter()).



Each Filter in the chain has, essentially, three possible behaviours:

Block the request: for example, 400 (invalid data), 401 (invalid identity) or 403 (authenticated but without permission)
Modify the request: data normalisation and validation, activity logging, among others
Let it proceed: by calling chain.doFilter(request, response), passing control to the next element in the chain

Consider an application with an authentication Filter in front of the Servlet that shows the user’s profile, mapped to /perfil. The path of a request is this:

The browser sends GET /perfil.
Before the request reaches the Servlet, the container hands it to the Filter, which looks for the session with getSession(false) and, inside it, the utilizador attribute.
No session (the user has not logged in yet): the Filter answers 401 and the request ends there. The Servlet never runs.
With a session: the Filter calls chain.doFilter(request, response) and the request goes on to the Servlet, which produces the profile page.
The Servlet’s response passes through the Filter again, on its way to the browser.

title: 6  Security and Filters
section: 6.5 The Life Cycle of a Filter
text:
6.5 The Life Cycle of a Filter
The life cycle of a Filter follows the same model already presented for Servlets (see Chapter 4):

init(): runs only once, when the container puts the Filter into service
doFilter(): runs on each request; it can inspect, block or modify the request and the response, and must call chain.doFilter() to continue the chain; it can also run code after chain.doFilter() returns, with the response already produced by the Servlet
destroy(): runs only once, when the Filter is taken out of service, to release resources

Like a Servlet, there is a single instance of each Filter, shared by multiple concurrent requests: exactly the same care already mentioned in Chapter 4 applies here, avoid shared mutable state and prefer local variables inside doFilter().






Figure 6.2: The life cycle of a Filter mirrors that of a Servlet: init() and destroy() run only once, doFilter() runs on every request, for multiple concurrent requests.

title: 6  Security and Filters
section: 6.6 Servlet and Filter: Separation of Responsibilities
text:
6.6 Servlet and Filter: Separation of Responsibilities
Centralising security in a Filter reorganises the responsibilities of the whole application:






Figure 6.3: Without a Filter, each Servlet accumulates authentication, logging, validation and business logic. With a Filter, those cross-cutting concerns are concentrated in a single place, and each Servlet keeps only its business logic.



This reorganisation brings concrete advantages:

The authentication logic is written only once (DRY principle)
The security policy is applied consistently to all endpoints
There is no longer a risk of “forgetting” the protection in a new Servlet
The separation between cross-cutting concerns (Filter) and business logic (Servlet) becomes clear

title: 6  Security and Filters
6  Security and Filters
text:
6.8 Redirect vs. 401: an Architectural Difference
The right way to react to an authentication failure depends on the type of application:

In a traditional, presentation-oriented Web application (see Chapter 1), the natural response is a redirect to the login page (code 302)
In a REST API, whose contract is JSON (see Chapters 7 and 8), the right response is to return 401, without any redirect

The difference boils down to one sentence: in a traditional Web application, an authentication failure changes the page shown; in a REST API, it changes only the status code returned. It is the client, not the server, that decides what to do next with that 401.

title: 6  Security and Filters
text:
6.9 Preparing for Stateless Security
The model presented in this chapter relies entirely on the session: the server keeps the authenticated user’s state (HttpSession), and the Filter checks that session on every request. This model has a limitation: it requires the server to keep a memory of each user, which becomes a problem as soon as there is more than one server handling requests (see Chapter 7).
The alternative is token-based authentication: instead of the server keeping any session, the request itself carries, on every call, all the information needed to authenticate itself. This change, from a stateful model to a stateless model, is the subject of the following chapters.

title: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)
text:
7.1 The Problem: Applications That Need to Communicate
So far, the server has always been thought of from the perspective of a single type of client: a browser, asking for HTML pages for a human user to read. But a server rarely serves only that type of client. A mobile application, another server, an integration script, or the JavaScript running in the browser itself (see Chapter 8) may also need to access the same information, without any of them needing, or wanting, to receive an HTML page ready to display.
HTML is a format designed for presentation: it mixes the data with the structure and with the way that data should be shown. A program that only needs the data (for example, the title and author of a book) would have to “take apart” the HTML to get to it, which is fragile and depends on presentation details that have nothing to do with the information itself. What is needed is a way of exposing the same data so that any program, and not only a browser with a human looking at it, can consume it directly.
crumbs: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)

title: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)
text:
7.2 What Is a Web Service
A Web Service is a software component accessible over the network, typically via HTTP, that exposes functionality or data in a format designed to be consumed by other programs, not by a human reading directly. Unlike a Web page, a Web Service does not generate presentation: it returns only the data, organised in a known structure, and it is the client that decides what to do with it.
This decoupling is what allows the same server to answer, with the same logic, requests coming from completely different sources: a mobile application, a JavaScript front-office, or another server. They all receive the same data, in the same structure, and each one decides how to present it (or whether to present it at all).
crumbs: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)

title: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)
text:
7.3 SOAP and REST: Two Approaches
Historically, there have been two main approaches to building Web Services:

SOAP (Simple Object Access Protocol)

A formal, XML-based protocol, with a rigid message structure (the SOAP envelope) and a contract described separately, in a WSDL document. It is verbose and requires specific tools to generate and consume that contract, but it offers strong formal guarantees. It is used mainly in legacy enterprise systems, with strict transaction and security requirements.

REST (Representational State Transfer)

An architectural style, not a formal protocol, that uses HTTP directly as transport and as contract: the methods, status codes and headers already presented in Chapters 3 and 4 are themselves the vocabulary of the API. It is lighter and simpler to test, and it is today the dominant approach in Web and mobile applications. It is the only one covered in detail in this course.
crumbs: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)

title: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)
text:
7.4 REST: Fielding’s Principles
The term REST was coined by Roy Fielding, in 2000, to describe the architectural style that was already, in practice, implicit in the design of the Web itself. A REST service follows a set of principles:

Client-server: responsibilities are separated; the client does not need to know how the data is stored, and the server does not need to know how it is presented.
Stateless: each request contains all the information needed to process it, without depending on memory of previous requests on the server (see Section 7.10).
Uniform interface: resources are always manipulated in the same way, through HTTP’s own methods and status codes, without inventing a vocabulary of its own for each API.
Resources and representations: everything the API exposes is modelled as a resource, identified by a URL, with one or more possible representations (typically JSON).
Cacheable: a response can indicate whether or not it may be cached, to avoid unnecessary repeated requests.

Not all APIs that call themselves “REST” respect all these principles rigorously. In practice, “REST” has become a generic term for “API over HTTP, resource-oriented, typically with JSON”, and that is the meaning used throughout this course.
crumbs: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)

title: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)
text:
7.5 Resource-Oriented Architecture
The most visible principle of REST is to think of the API in terms of resources, not actions. A resource is anything that can be identified and manipulated (a book, an author, an order) and is identified by a URL, never by a function name.
A design that does not follow this principle is closer to an RPC (Remote Procedure Call) style, in which the URL names an operation:

GET /obterLivro?id=12
GET /removerLivro?id=12

A resource-oriented design uses the URL itself to identify the resource, and lets the HTTP method (see Chapter 3) indicate the operation to perform on it:

GET /livros/12 → get book 12
DELETE /livros/12 → remove book 12

The advantage is not merely aesthetic: it makes the API predictable. Once the /livros/{id} pattern is known, it is immediately clear how to get, update or remove any book, without having to memorise a different function name for each operation. The same pattern applies to any other resource: /autores/3, /encomendas/5.
crumbs: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)

title: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)
section: 7.6 HTTP Methods as the API Contract
text:
7.6 HTTP Methods as the API Contract
In a REST API, HTTP methods are no longer just “the way the request arrives” (see Chapter 3) and become the API contract itself: the meaning of each method, applied to a resource, is always the same.



Method
Example
Operation
Idempotent?




GET
GET /livros/12
Read the resource
Yes


POST
POST /livros
Create a new resource
No


PUT
PUT /livros/12
Update or replace the resource
Yes


DELETE
DELETE /livros/12
Remove the resource
Yes



A method is said to be idempotent when repeating it several times has exactly the same effect as executing it once. DELETE /livros/12 removes book 12; repeating the same request does not remove “anything else”, and the end result is identical. POST /livros, on the other hand, creates a new book on each call, so it is not idempotent: repeating the request creates several books, not just one. This property matters above all on unreliable networks. A client that is not sure whether a PUT or DELETE request reached its destination can safely repeat it; with a POST it cannot, or it risks duplicating the created resource.






POST + operation as an alternative to “pure” HTTP methods



In practice, it is common to find APIs that do not follow the “pure” semantics of the HTTP methods presented above (POST to create, PUT to update, DELETE to remove). A pragmatic alternative, used mainly when only GET and POST requests can be issued (as from a plain HTML form, without JavaScript, see Chapter 2), is to concentrate the write operations in a single endpoint, always received by POST, and to distinguish the intended operation through an additional parameter, such as operation (insert, update, delete).
This solution works, but it departs from the more conventional REST design: a single endpoint no longer corresponds directly to a resource and a method, and gets closer to an RPC style over HTTP. In an API designed to be consumed by JavaScript, which can issue PUT and DELETE requests without any limitation (see Chapter 8), the alternative closest to REST is to split that endpoint into several, one per HTTP method (for example, PUT /livros/{id} to update and DELETE /livros/{id} to remove).
crumbs: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)

title: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)
text:
7.7 The REST Contract: HTTP Semantics
In SOAP, the contract is explicit: to know how to call a service, one has to read the WSDL document that describes it. In REST, the contract is implicit: it is already defined by HTTP itself, complemented by a few conventions. Besides the methods, two parts of HTTP belong to this contract:

Status codes tell the client what happened to the request, without having to read the response body.
Headers carry the metadata: the body format (Content-Type), its size, or the identification of who is making the request.

The status codes most used in a REST API are these (see Chapter 3):








Code
Meaning in a REST API
Example




200 OK
The request went well; the body carries the result
GET /livros/12


201 Created
The resource was created
POST /livros


400 Bad Request
The data sent is invalid
POST /livros without a title


401 Unauthorized
The request is not authenticated
any protected request, without authentication


404 Not Found
The resource does not exist
GET /livros/99, if there is no book 99



A client asking for a book that does not exist sends this request:

GET /livros/99 HTTP/1.1
Host: exemplo.pt

and receives a response whose meaning is clear from the first line alone:

HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found

Whoever understands HTTP understands the API: the same knowledge works for any REST API, without having to learn a new contract for each one.
crumbs: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)

title: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)
section: 7.8 JSON as the Representation of a Resource
text:
7.8 JSON as the Representation of a Resource
A resource can have more than one possible representation: the same book could, in theory, be returned in JSON, in XML, or in any other format, depending on what the client asks for. In practice, and throughout this course, the representation used is always JSON, a lightweight, easy-to-read format, independent of the programming language (the format traditionally associated with SOAP is XML, more verbose and less direct to generate and interpret in JavaScript).
The response to GET /livros/12 is, for example, this representation of the book:
{"id": 12, "titulo": "Os Maias", "autor": "Eça de Queirós"}
The Content-Type: application/json header (see Chapter 4) is what informs the client that this is the representation chosen for the response. In a REST API, neither objects nor pages are transferred, but representations of the state of each resource.
crumbs: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)

title: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)
section: 7.9 From a Web Application to a REST Service
text:
7.9 From a Web Application to a REST Service
The infrastructure behind a REST service is not new: it is still a Servlet, mapped to a URL through @WebServlet (see Chapter 4), receiving an HTTP request and returning a response. What changes is what that response contains, and who it is meant for.
In a presentation-oriented application (see Chapters 1 and 5), the Servlet returns HTML, meant for a human to read directly in the browser. In a REST API, the same Servlet returns JSON, meant to be interpreted by code: another server, a mobile application, or the browser’s own JavaScript (see Chapter 8). The View, in the classic MVC sense (see Chapter 1), no longer exists on the server side: it is the client, whatever it is, that decides how (or whether) to present the data received.






Figure 7.1: In a Web application, the View (JSP) lives on the server and generates the HTML; in a REST API, the server returns only JSON and it is the client’s JavaScript that draws the page.
crumbs: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)

title: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)
text:
7.10 Stateful vs. Stateless
Chapter 5 presented a stateful model: the server keeps, in the HttpSession, information about each authenticated user, and each following request is interpreted in the light of that memory. A stateless service follows the opposite principle: the server keeps no memory at all between requests, and each request must carry, in itself, all the information needed to process it, including, if necessary, the proof that whoever makes it is authenticated.
This does not mean that the application as a whole stops having persistent data: the database still keeps books, authors and orders. It only means that the application server itself keeps no session information about who is making each request, between one request and the next.

title: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)
section: 7.11 Why the Absence of State Matters
text:
7.11 Why the Absence of State Matters
The limitation of the stateful model only becomes visible when there is more than one server handling requests (several Tomcats, each with the same application installed; not to be confused with instances of a Servlet, of which there is always only one per Tomcat, see Chapter 4), a common situation in any application with a real need to scale. Requests first reach a load balancer, which distributes them among the various servers. The path of two consecutive requests shows where the problem lies:

The user logs in; the load balancer sends the request to server A, which creates the session in its memory.
The next request, GET /livros, is sent by the load balancer to server B.
Server B has no corresponding session in its memory: the user appears as not authenticated (401), despite having just logged in.







Figure 7.2: With a session, server B does not know the session created on server A and answers 401; without state, the request itself carries the proof of authentication and any server can answer.



A stateless service does not suffer from this problem: since no server keeps a memory of anyone, any of them can answer any request. This property is what makes it possible to distribute requests among several servers without any coordination between them, a subject taken up in detail in Chapter 8.
crumbs: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)

title: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)
text:
7.12 Monolith and Microservices
The absence of state has consequences for the way an application is organised. In a monolith, the application is a single unit of deployment, often stateful (the session lives in the server’s memory), and it can only be scaled as a whole. In a microservices architecture, the application is split into small, independent services, which communicate with each other through REST APIs, without state and with token authentication, and each one can scale on its own. The absence of state is what makes it possible to spread an application across several servers and several services.
crumbs: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)

title: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)
text:
7.13 REST and RESTful
REST is an architectural style: stateless, resource-oriented and with a uniform interface. A RESTful API is an API that claims to follow that style. Since the absence of state is part of the very definition of REST, an API that keeps the user’s session on the server is not fully RESTful.
One question is therefore left open: if the server keeps no state at all, how does it know, on each request, who the user is? The answer, token authentication, is the subject of Chapter 8.
crumbs: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)

title: 8  REST Web Services (Part 2) and the JavaScript Client
text:
8.1 Limitations of Sessions in Distributed Systems
A web application with many users has to scale, that is, to cope with more work (more users, more requests per second) without slowing down or stopping. There are two ways of doing it:
The difference is the same as in a supermarket: instead of having a single checkout operator who gets faster and faster (vertical), more checkouts are opened, with a single queue that sends each customer to the first free checkout (horizontal). For this to work, any checkout has to be able to serve any customer. Web applications with many users scale horizontally, and that is where sessions cause problems.
Chapter 7 ended by pointing out that problem: an authentication model based on HttpSession (see Chapter 5) requires the server to keep, in memory, the state of each authenticated user. As soon as there is more than one server (several Tomcats, each with the same application installed, behind a load balancer that distributes the requests), that memory is no longer automatically shared among them. This is not about several instances of the same Servlet: inside a Tomcat, simultaneous requests are handled by several threads of the same instance (see Chapter 4), which share the same memory and therefore the same sessions.
There are well-known workarounds for this problem (Figure 8.1), sticky sessions (always routing the same client to the same server) and session replication between servers, but both have a cost: the first limits how requests can be distributed, and the second requires extra infrastructure just to keep the servers in sync. Neither solves the problem at its root; both are ways of working around a dependency on state that, for a REST API (see Chapter 7), should not even exist.
crumbs: 8  REST Web Services (Part 2) and the JavaScript Client

title: 8  REST Web Services (Part 2) and the JavaScript Client
text:
Vertical scalability

Giving more resources (processors, memory) to the same machine. It is simple, because the application does not change, but it has a physical limit and does not solve the problem of the single point of failure: if that single machine breaks down or has to be restarted, the whole application becomes unavailable

Horizontal scalability

Adding more identical servers, running in parallel, with a load balancer distributing the requests among them. It has almost no limit, because more servers can simply be added, and, if one fails, the others keep answering











Figure 8.1: The two workarounds: with sticky sessions, the load balancer always sends the same user to the server that holds her session; with replication, the servers copy the sessions to each other and any of them can answer.
crumbs: 8  REST Web Services (Part 2) and the JavaScript Client

title: 8  REST Web Services (Part 2) and the JavaScript Client
text:
8.2 Stateless Authentication: the Authorization Header
The stateless alternative reverses the responsibility: instead of the server keeping track of who is authenticated, it is the client itself that keeps a proof of its authentication, a token, and sends it back with each request, typically in the HTTP Authorization header:

Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOiJhbmEiLCJyb2xlIjoidXNlciIsImV4cCI6MTg5MzQ1NjAwMH0.O1M0ymsf-ceCK3OxAewCVLReDaVliYUirWclbBC4-LE

The Authorization header is not exclusive to tokens: the HTTP standard always defines it with the format Authorization: <scheme> <credentials>, and the first word, the scheme, tells the server how to interpret what follows.



Table 8.1: Some schemes of the Authorization header.










Scheme
What follows
Example




Basic
user:password in Base64
Authorization: Basic YW5hOnNlZ3JlZG8=


Bearer
a token (for example, a JWT)
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...


Digest
a digest computed from the password
rarely used today






Without the scheme, the server would not know whether eyJhbGciOi... is a token, an encoded password or something else; it is also a convention followed by clients, libraries and servers, which write and expect Bearer <token>. The word Bearer literally means “bearer”: whoever presents this token is treated as its rightful owner, with no further questions. That is why the token must always travel over HTTPS and must never be exposed. On receiving the request, the server does not need to look anything up in memory: it only has to validate the token itself. What it is, and how that validation works, is the subject of the next section.
crumbs: 8  REST Web Services (Part 2) and the JavaScript Client

title: 8  REST Web Services (Part 2) and the JavaScript Client
text:
8.3 JWT: a Stateless Token
A JSON Web Token (JWT) is a standardised token format, designed to carry information in a compact and verifiable way, without the server needing to store anything about it. A JWT always has three parts, separated by dots:
<header>.<payload>.<signature>

Header

Metadata about the token itself, for example {"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}: alg indicates the signature algorithm (HS256 is an HMAC with SHA-256); typ indicates that it is a JWT, is optional and, in practice, almost always has this value

Payload

The data the token carries, the claims (statements about the user), for example {"sub":"ana","role":"user","exp":1893456000}. sub (subject) indicates who the user is; role is their profile, a claim defined by the application itself; exp (expiration) is the moment until which the token is valid, counted in seconds since 1 January 1970 (here, 1 January 2030)

Signature

The result of cryptographically signing the header and the payload with a secret key, known only to the server


Each of these three parts is encoded in Base64URL and joined with dots, resulting in the long, unreadable string typical of a JWT (like the one in the Authorization header example above). Base64 writes any data using only 64 safe characters (upper- and lower-case letters, digits and two more symbols): every 3 bytes become 4 characters. The Base64URL variant replaces those two symbols, + and /, with - and _, and drops the = padding at the end, so that the result can go in a URL or an HTTP header without being altered. Encoding is not encrypting: anyone can reverse it. For example, the text Ana (3 bytes) is encoded as QW5h (4 characters), and QW5h turns back into Ana with no key at all (Figure 8.2). Likewise, {"alg":"HS256",...} gives eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIs..., which is why every JWT starts with eyJ (the initial {", encoded: the 8 bits of the brace are split between the e and part of the y, because Base64 converts bits, not characters one by one).
There are three reasons for using this encoding in a JWT. The signature is raw bytes (32, in the case of HS256), with values that do not correspond to any printable character and cannot go into an HTTP header as they are. The JSON of the header and the payload contains characters such as {, ", :, spaces or accented letters, some of which have a special meaning in a URL or a header. And, since . is not one of the 64 Base64URL characters, it can serve as an unambiguous separator between the three parts. Base64 neither protects nor compresses: anyone can decode it, and the result is about a third larger than the original.






Figure 8.2: Base64 step by step: the 3 bytes of Ana (65, 110 and 97) make 24 bits; read in 4 groups of 6 bits, they are worth 16, 22, 57 and 33, which in the Base64 table correspond to Q, W, 5 and h.



The header and the payload are only encoded, not encrypted: anyone can read them, without needing any key. What ensures that nobody can forge a valid token is the signature: only whoever knows the server’s secret key can generate it correctly, and any change to the header or the payload, however small, invalidates the signature. On receiving a request, the server recomputes the signature from the header and payload received, and compares it with the one that came in the token: if they match, the content can be trusted, without the server having had to store absolutely anything itself (Figure 8.3).






Figure 8.3: The three parts of a real JWT, all in Base64URL: the header and the payload decode into JSON that anyone can read; the signature decodes into 32 unreadable bytes, computed with the server’s secret key, and it is the signature that prevents the token from being forged.



In the HS256 algorithm, the signature is an HMAC with SHA-256: a 32-byte code computed from the already encoded header and payload (header.payload) and from the secret key. Those 32 bytes are also carried in the token in Base64URL; decoded, they give no text at all, only raw bytes. Since the same key is used both to generate and to verify the signature, only the server should know it.

section: 8.5 The Great Advantage of JWT: Scaling Without State
text:
8.5 The Great Advantage of JWT: Scaling Without State
Horizontal scalability (see Section 8.1) only works smoothly when any server can answer any request, indiscriminately. With sessions, this requires sticky sessions or replication; with JWT-based authentication, it happens naturally: the state travels in the request itself, no server needs to know anything about any other, and each one validates the token received completely independently, with the same secret key shared by all (Figure 8.6). This is the main advantage of JWT over sessions, and the reason why REST APIs use tokens instead of sessions.






Figure 8.6: No state on the server: the login is handled by server A, the next request lands on server B, and B answers 200 because the request itself carries the token.
crumbs: 8  REST Web Services (Part 2) and the JavaScript Client

title: 8  REST Web Services (Part 2) and the JavaScript Client
text:
8.6 JWT and Microservices
The same logic applies, even more strongly, to an application split into microservices (see Section 7.12): instead of a single web application, there are several small services, each one a web application of its own (for example, an authentication service, a books service and an orders service), installed on the same server, on different ports or paths, or on different servers.
With sessions, each service would have its own sessions: the JSESSIONID created by the authentication service means nothing to the books service, which would have to ask for the credentials again or ask the first service, on every request, who that user is. With JWT, the client logs in only once, at the authentication service, and sends the same token to all the others; each service checks the signature on its own, without asking anyone (Figure 8.7). Each service can also scale independently of the others: if the books service is the most requested, servers are added just for it.






Figure 8.7: JWT with microservices: the client logs in at the authentication service, receives the JWT and sends it to the books and orders services, which validate it without consulting the authentication service.



There is one precaution: with HS256, all the services would have to know the secret key and, with it, any of them could issue tokens. In systems with several services, an asymmetric algorithm (RS256 or ES256) is therefore used: only the authentication service signs, with a private key, and the others only verify, with the corresponding public key (see Section B.3).

title: 8  REST Web Services (Part 2) and the JavaScript Client
section: 8.8 Distributed MVC: the Pattern Splits Between Server and Client
text:
8.8 Distributed MVC: the Pattern Splits Between Server and Client
In a presentation-oriented application, the MVC pattern (see Chapter 1) lives entirely on the server side: one component works as Controller, and another, responsible for generating HTML, as View. In a REST API, that organisation no longer makes sense: the server no longer generates HTML, and the View, as defined in classic MVC, disappears from the server side.
On the server side, only the Model (data access) and the Controller (the endpoint that receives the HTTP request and returns JSON) remain. The role of View passes entirely to the client: it is the JavaScript code, running in the browser, that interprets the JSON received and manipulates the DOM to present it to whoever uses the application.
This split can be read as a second application of the same pattern, now on the client side: the JavaScript that handles the response and updates the page works, itself, as Controller (it decides what to do with the response received) and as View (it generates the HTML shown); the JSON returned by the API is the Model, kept on the server and synchronised with each fetch() request.
This is why a JavaScript front-office connected to a REST API is not an alternative to MVC, but the same pattern distributed across two machines instead of one.
