title: Appendix B — JWT Token Signing
text:
B.1 Introduction
Chapter 8 showed how a JWT (see Section 8.3) is signed and verified, without ever going into detail on which algorithm is used, or what security guarantees that signature actually offers. This appendix looks specifically at that question: token signing.

title: Appendix B — JWT Token Signing
section: B.2 HMAC: a Shared Secret Key
text:
B.2 HMAC: a Shared Secret Key
The algorithm used in Chapter 8, HS256, is the combination of HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code) with the SHA-256 cryptographic hash function. It is a symmetric algorithm: the same secret key is used both to sign and to verify a token.
That key is never generated on the client, nor does it ever travel to it: it is created and stored exclusively on the server (typically once, during the application’s initial setup), and never leaves it. What the client receives, and later resends, is always the already-signed token — the result of using the key — never the key itself.






Figure B.1: In a symmetric scheme (HMAC), the same server holds the single secret key that exists, and uses it both to sign the token at login and to verify it on every subsequent request.



This works well in exactly the situation presented throughout this course: a single server (or several servers running the same application, all with access to the same secret key, see Section 8.5) is, at the same time, the one that issues tokens and the one that validates them. The key never leaves that trust boundary.
The drawback of HMAC appears when that boundary stops making sense: if an external system — one that should not have the authority to issue valid tokens — needed to validate them, it would have to receive the same secret key used to sign them. At that point, it stops being just a verifier: it also becomes capable of forging new, valid tokens, for any user.

title: Appendix B — JWT Token Signing
section: B.3 RSA and ECDSA: a Key Pair
text:
B.3 RSA and ECDSA: a Key Pair
An asymmetric algorithm solves this problem by splitting the two capabilities into two distinct keys: a private key, known only to whoever issues tokens, and a corresponding public key, which can be freely distributed to whoever needs to validate them. What the private key signs can only be verified with the corresponding public key — but it is not possible to sign anything new using only the public key.
The two most common asymmetric algorithms in JWT are RS256 (RSA with SHA-256) and ES256 (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm with SHA-256) — the latter more recent, with smaller keys and faster verification for an equivalent security level, increasingly preferred over RSA in new systems.






Figure B.2: In an asymmetric scheme (RSA/ECDSA), only the Authentication Service holds the private key and signs new tokens; the corresponding public key can be freely distributed to any server that only needs to validate, without ever being able to issue tokens on another’s behalf.



This design is the usual one in systems made up of several independent services (sometimes called microservices): a single Authentication Service, responsible for validating credentials and issuing tokens, and several other services, each validating those tokens completely on its own, without ever communicating with each other, or trusting each other beyond the shared public key.

title: Appendix B — JWT Token Signing
section: B.4 Choosing Between HMAC and Asymmetric Signing
text:
B.4 Choosing Between HMAC and Asymmetric Signing









HMAC (HS256)
Asymmetric (RS256/ES256)




Number of keys
One, shared
Two: private (issues) and public (verifies)


Who can issue valid tokens
Anyone with the key
Only whoever has the private key


Who can validate tokens
Anyone with the key
Anyone with the public key


Typical scenario
One server (or trusted cluster) issues and validates
Several independent services only validate


Performance
Faster, simpler
Slower, larger keys (except ECDSA)



For the “World Capitals” application used throughout this course — a single server, responsible both for issuing and for validating its own tokens — HMAC is a perfectly adequate choice, which is why Chapter 8 uses it as its example. The choice would only start to favour an asymmetric algorithm if the application grew into several independent services, each of which should be able to validate, but not issue, access credentials.

title: Appendix B — JWT Token Signing
text:
B.5 The alg:none Attack
The header of a JWT itself declares which algorithm was used for the signature (see Section 8.3). The original JWT specification allows, among the possible values for that field, the value none — intended for cases where integrity is already guaranteed by some other mechanism, and no signature is even needed.
A poorly implemented verifier, one that blindly trusts the algorithm declared in the header instead of enforcing an expected algorithm, can be fooled by a token like this one:
{"alg": "none", "typ": "JWT"}
followed by an arbitrary payload and an empty signature. If the verification code does not explicitly reject the none algorithm, an attacker can build, by hand, a token with any payload they want — for example, {"sub":"admin","role":"admin"} — without needing to know any key at all, and the server accepts it as legitimate.
It is exactly this attack that motivates the recommendation already made in Chapter 8: a well-written library, such as JJWT, requires the expected algorithm to be stated explicitly in the verification code, and rejects any token that declares a different algorithm — including none — regardless of what the token itself claims about itself.

title: Appendix B — JWT Token Signing
section: B.6 Where to Store the Token on the Client
text:
B.6 Where to Store the Token on the Client
Everything covered so far protects the token against forgery — but not against theft (see Section 8.2): whoever holds it can use it freely, as if they were its rightful owner, until it expires. Where the client stores it between requests determines what kind of theft it is exposed to.

Storing it in the browser’s localStorage

Accessible to any JavaScript code running on the page — including, unfortunately, a malicious script injected through a Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability. If such a vulnerability exists in the application, an attacker can read the token directly and resend it, impersonating the user. On the other hand, it is not automatically sent by the browser in requests to other sites, so it is not exposed to Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)

HttpOnly cookie

Marked with the HttpOnly attribute, a cookie becomes inaccessible to the page’s own JavaScript — not even a malicious script can read it, which neutralises theft via XSS. In exchange, the browser automatically resends cookies on any request to the domain, even when that request is triggered by a page from another site — reopening the door to CSRF, which then has to be mitigated separately (for example, with the SameSite attribute)






localStorage
HttpOnly cookie




Accessible to JavaScript
Yes
No


Vulnerable to XSS theft
Yes
No


Automatically resent by the browser
No
Yes


Vulnerable to CSRF
No
Yes, requires separate mitigation



Neither option is risk-free — each trades one kind of vulnerability for another. The model followed in Chapter 8 (token resent manually in the Authorization header, see Section 8.9) assumes the token is accessible to the page’s own JavaScript, which points to localStorage, and is the most common approach in modern single-page applications. In that model, preventing XSS stops being just a general best practice: it becomes an essential condition for the security of the authentication mechanism itself — even though preventing XSS itself falls outside the scope of this appendix.

title: Appendix B — JWT Token Signing
text:
B.7 Minimum Best Practices

Never blindly accept the token’s declared algorithm — the verification code must explicitly enforce the expected algorithm (see Section B.5)
The secret (HMAC) or private (RSA/ECDSA) key must never live in the source code — it should be read from an environment variable or a dedicated secrets manager, never committed to a repository
A short or predictable key defeats the algorithm’s security — the recommended minimum length depends on the algorithm, but a short, memorable string is never appropriate
A short expiry (the exp claim, see Section 8.4) limits the damage from a compromised token, even with no additional mechanism
HTTPS is always mandatory — even a correctly signed token is a valid credential if it is intercepted in transit; the signature protects against forgery, not against network eavesdropping

These practices are a starting point, not an exhaustive treatment of Web application security.

section: C.2 The Tools for This Course
text:
C.2 The Tools for This Course

JDK — Java Development Kit

The Java language and the tools to compile and run it — the foundation for everything else. The Eclipse Temurin distribution is recommended: free, open source, maintained by the Eclipse Adoptium Working Group, and available for all three operating systems. Alternative: Oracle JDK, Oracle’s official build, under a different licence. Help: official documentation at https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/; for specific questions, the java tag on Stack Overflow is the first place to check.

Apache Tomcat

The Servlet Container used throughout the course (see Chapter 4), installed on the server side. Available at https://tomcat.apache.org/. Alternatives exist (Jetty, or a full application server such as WildFly, already mentioned in Chapter 4), but they are not used in this course. Help: official documentation at https://tomcat.apache.org/tomcat-10.1-doc/; the tomcat tag on Stack Overflow for specific questions.

Eclipse IDE for Enterprise Java and Web Developers

The development environment (IDE) used for server-side code (Servlets, Filters, JSP), with built-in support for Jakarta EE projects and for installing and managing Tomcat directly from within Eclipse. Downloaded from https://www.eclipse.org/downloads/packages/ (choose exactly the “Enterprise Java and Web Developers” package, not the generic “Eclipse IDE for Java Developers” package, which does not include the Web project tools). Alternative: IntelliJ IDEA (the Ultimate edition, paid — but free for students on registration — includes equivalent Jakarta EE support; the free Community edition does not). Help: Eclipse community forum; the eclipse tag on Stack Overflow.

VSCode or WebStorm

A lighter editor, used for client-side code (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, see Chapter 2 and Chapter 8) — it does not need either of Eclipse’s two Java EE-specific supports. VSCode is free and cross-platform; WebStorm is paid (free for students on registration), more specialised in JavaScript. Help: official documentation at https://code.visualstudio.com/docs (VSCode) or https://www.jetbrains.com/webstorm/documentation/ (WebStorm).

A modern browser, with developer tools

Chrome, Firefox and Edge all work equally well; what matters is knowing how to open their developer tools (DevTools, F12 key or Cmd+Option+I on Mac), used throughout the course to inspect network requests and debug JavaScript (see Chapter 8). Help: https://developer.chrome.com/docs/devtools/ (Chrome) or https://firefox-source-docs.mozilla.org/devtools-user/ (Firefox).

A REST client

A tool for building HTTP requests by hand (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, with headers and body of your choosing), useful for testing a REST API directly (see Chapter 7) without depending on any front-office already built. A simple GET can always be tested directly in the browser, but POST, PUT and DELETE cannot. Yaak is recommended: a lightweight, open-source application, free for personal use, that reaches Tomcat directly on localhost. Whoever prefers not to install anything else can use the VSCode REST Client extension: requests are written in a .http file, as text, in the same format as the HTTP messages of Chapter 3, and each one is sent with a click. Hoppscotch works directly in the browser, but can only reach a server on localhost once its browser extension or the Hoppscotch Agent is installed. Whoever prefers the command line can use curl, already included by default on macOS, on Linux, and on Windows 10 and later.

MySQL or MariaDB

The relational database management system used from LAB4 onward (Appendix G), when the fixed data used in the earlier LABs is replaced with real data, accessed through JDBC. MySQL Community Server is the free, open-source edition of MySQL; MariaDB Server is a free, open-source alternative, directly compatible (same network protocol, same JDBC driver) — either one works for this course. To create and manage the tables without relying solely on the command line, it is also useful to install a graphical client, such as MySQL Workbench or DBeaver (cross-platform, compatible with both MySQL and MariaDB). Help: official documentation at https://dev.mysql.com/doc/ (MySQL) or https://mariadb.com/kb/en/documentation/ (MariaDB); the mysql and mariadb tags on Stack Overflow for specific questions.

title: Appendix D — LAB1: First Endpoint and Simulated DAO
section: D.2 LAB1: First Endpoint and Simulated DAO
text:
D.2 LAB1: First Endpoint and Simulated DAO
A good development environment setup is the foundation of any robust, maintainable application. Investing time up front in correctly preparing the tools and structuring the project saves, later on, countless hours of debugging and reorganising. This LAB guides the configuration of Eclipse and Tomcat, and the creation of the first endpoint, which will serve as the API’s “health check”.

D.2.1 Step 1.1: Prepare the Development Environment

Install the Eclipse IDE: start by downloading and installing “Eclipse IDE for Enterprise Java and Web Developers” (see Appendix C). It is important to choose exactly this edition, since it comes pre-configured with the essential tools for this project
Install Apache Tomcat (see Appendix C for the required version), following the installation instructions, outside Eclipse
Configure Apache Tomcat in Eclipse:

In Eclipse, go to the Servers perspective. If it is not visible, open it via Window > Show View > Servers
Click the link to create a new server (“No servers are available. Click this link to create a new server…”)
In the window that appears, expand the Apache folder and select the installed Tomcat version
Follow the wizard’s steps, pointing to the folder where Tomcat was installed
Once finished, the Tomcat server appears in the Servers perspective, ready to use




D.2.2 Step 1.2: Create the Dynamic Web Project

From the Eclipse menu, select File > New > Dynamic Web Project
In the project creation window, set the Project name to CapitaisAPI
Confirm that the Target runtime is set to the Apache Tomcat server configured in the previous step
Click Finish to create the project
Once the project is created, it is good practice to organise the source code into packages: in the Project Explorer, expand the “Java Resources” section and locate the source folder (usually src or src/main/java). Right-click that folder, New > Package, and create the package capitaisapi.servlets



D.2.3 Step 1.3: Develop the First Endpoint (Servlet)
The first endpoint is a simple status checker, to confirm that the API is working correctly.

Right-click the capitaisapi.servlets package just created, New > Servlet
In the window that opens, keep all fields at their pre-filled value, and name the class StatusServlet. Click Finish
Eclipse generates the class skeleton. Map this Servlet to the /status URL through the @WebServlet annotation, directly above the class declaration (it becomes @WebServlet("/status"))
Test the Servlet: in the file explorer, right-click the file containing the Servlet, Run As > Run on Server. Choose the Tomcat server of the same version used when creating the Servlet, and Finish. Within a few seconds, the Servlet’s result should appear in a browser
Create a new Servlet, following the same process, in the same package, called CountryCapital, and change the doGet method to return a simple JSON message. This method is invoked whenever an HTTP GET request is made to the /countrycapital URL. To write this method according to HTTP requirements and good programming practice (see Chapter 4), replace all of doGet()’s code with this:

// Inside the doGet method of the CountryCapital Servlet
response.setContentType("application/json"); // sets the content type to JSON
PrintWriter out = response.getWriter(); // obtains the output stream

// Manual construction of the JSON String
String jsonResponse = "{\"country\": \"Portugal\", \"capital\": \"Lisboa\", \"ccode\": \"PT\"}";
out.print(jsonResponse); // sends the structured data to the client
out.flush();
PrintWriter needs to be imported, since it is not included in the Servlet’s generated skeleton. Note that the JSON String contains quotes inside it — so the quotes inside the Java String have to be written as \" (escaped). Do not use single quotes inside the String, since they are not valid in JSON.


D.2.4 Step 1.4: Deploy and Test the Application

Test the Servlet again, exactly as in Step 1.3 (point 4). Eclipse compiles, deploys and starts the application on the server
It is also possible to test by right-clicking the project name (CapitaisAPI) — this opens a browser (or a testing tool). Enter the following URL:
http://localhost:8080/CapitaisAPI/countrycapital
The following response should appear on screen:
{"country": "Portugal", "capital": "Lisboa", "ccode": "PT"}

confirming that the first endpoint is working correctly. While the Servlet is running on the server, the browser can be closed and reopened, entering the same URL, and the result stays the same.


D.2.5 Step 1.5: Implement the Database Interface via a DAO
In a “real-life” application, dynamic content is normally generated from data coming from a database. The link between the Web application and the database can be made through a Data Access Object (DAO, see Chapter 4), which hides the database’s implementation details from the Web application. This application will use a DAO to interface between the Web application and the database.
Since there is no access to a real database yet, this stage of the project will use a DAO that simulates access to the database (later, in LAB4, this DAO will be changed to query a real database). Note that, from the Web application’s point of view, there is no difference at all between a DAO that fetches data from a real database and one that has the data fixed directly in the code.
Create a new class, called DBDAO, in the capitaisapi.dao package, and write three public methods in it:

List<String> getCountryCodes();
String getCountryName(String countryCode);
String getCapitalName(String countryCode);

The first method returns the list of available country codes (PT, FR, EN, etc.), the second returns the country name associated with a code, and the last returns the capital name associated with a country code.
For this LAB, fix all return values directly in the DBDAO class’s code. Use a HashMap<String, String> to hold the fixed values of country codes and capital names, and a List to hold the list of country codes.
By default, the /countrycapital Servlet should show the capital of the first country in the list returned by the DAO’s List<String> getCountryCodes() method.


D.2.6 Step 1.6: Create the Data Model (POJO)
To represent the application’s data in a structured way, POJOs (Plain Old Java Objects) are used. A POJO is a data type, just like String or Integer, and so it helps guarantee that a given piece of information always follows the same rules. If a POJO is used as a method’s return value, that value comes to respect what is defined in the POJO — in other words, a POJO is a data model. It is created already at this stage, so that the main pieces are defined, even though the POJO will only actually be used further on.

Create a new class called CountryModel in the capitaisapi.servlets package. This will be the POJO
Add private attributes to represent a country’s data: codigo, nome and capital. Later, if convenient, others can be added, such as population or area
Generate the getters and setters for all attributes: right-click a blank line below the attribute definitions, Source > Generate Getters and Setters — Eclipse generates the code automatically



D.2.7 Step 1.7: Develop the Capitals Endpoint
A new Servlet is now created that uses the DAO to return dynamic data. For testing purposes, the DAO should not return all of a country’s information (code, name and capital) — the POJO is only used when it is necessary to return a country’s complete information.

Create a new Servlet called CapitalServlet, in the capitaisapi.servlets package, mapped to the /capital URL
In the doGet method, implement the logic to:

Read the countrycode parameter from the request (request.getParameter("countrycode"))
Instantiate DBDAO and call getCapitalName() with the received country code
Check whether the country was found: if so, build a JSON String with the country code and the capital name; if not, return an appropriate error response. If the countrycode parameter is null or empty, return 400 (missing parameter, see Chapter 3); if countrycode has an unknown value, return 404 (country not found). Use response.setStatus(HttpServletResponse.SC_BAD_REQUEST) for 400, and response.setStatus(HttpServletResponse.SC_NOT_FOUND) for 404
Set the Content-Type to application/json, and send the JSON String as the response




D.2.8 Step 1.8: Develop the Countries Endpoint

Create a new Servlet CountryServlet, in the same package as the previous ones, mapped to /country
In DBDAO, add a new method CountryModel getCountry(String countrycode), meant to return all of a country’s data (code, country name and capital name)
Using a structure similar to CapitalServlet’s, in the doGet method, obtain a country’s complete data and return the complete JSON structure, properly validated by the CountryModel POJO

Note that the Servlet no longer manipulates isolated data (loose Strings), and instead works with a structured object — which improves readability, maintainability and data validation. The getCountry() method in DBDAO now centralises the aggregation of the data and encapsulates it in a structured model (POJO), reducing the Servlet’s responsibility.

E.1 LAB2: Login and Session
Security is a fundamental concern in any Web application. Since this is a REST API, redirects are not used as in a traditional Web application — all communication with the client happens through HTTP status codes and JSON bodies (see Chapter 3). In this LAB, a login endpoint is added to the “World Capitals API”, and the HTTP session (see Chapter 5) is used to keep track, on the server side, of the fact that a given user is authenticated.

title: Appendix H — LAB5 (Optional): Stateless Authentication with JWT
text:
H.1 LAB5 (Optional): Stateless Authentication with JWT
In LABs 1 to 4, server-side stateful authentication was implemented (HttpSession). This model is common in traditional Java Web applications, and is a good way of clearly understanding authentication and authorization.
In this optional LAB, the project evolves towards a modern, stateless REST API architecture: HttpSession and JSESSIONID are no longer used, the server stops keeping any per-user state between requests, and authentication is instead done with a JWT (JSON Web Token, see Chapter 8 and Appendix B), sent with every protected request. This LAB is optional, aimed at anyone who wants to go further and understand how modern APIs typically authenticate clients.
Objectives: by the end of this LAB, it should be possible to explain the difference between stateful (session) authentication and stateless (token) authentication; implement JWT-based authentication; use the HTTP Authorization header with the Bearer scheme; validate a JWT inside a Filter; and correctly distinguish 401 from 403.
